unit: per job: one rear crankshaft oil seal (the rear main seal), the round seal at the back of the engine where the crankshaft meets the transmission. The transmission has to come out, and the flexplate or flywheel has to come off, to reach it, so labor is nearly the whole bill and the seal itself is a small part. Priced here as the seal alone. Not included: a seal housing or retainer plate (on some engines the seal is only sold fitted to its housing or cover, which costs more), transmission fluid, a clutch or flywheel on manual cars, an oil pan gasket, or engine oil and filter (see extras)

benchmarks.name: ThePricer
benchmarks.note: 'Rear main seal replacement usually costs about $650 to $1,500 for many vehicles'; also says 'A typical job can require about 6 to 10 labor hours'. A general consumer pricing site: signed by a named author with no stated automotive credentials, updated August 19, 2026. The weakest of the three benchmarks

finding: The live range of $400-$1,925 is too low at the bottom for most cars and about right at the top, as far as we could check. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Cruze 1.4L, $16.15-$26.74 + 5.6-7.4 hr = about $688-$1,211; midsize 2016 Accord 2.4L, $17.04-$24.07 + 5.6-10 hr = about $689-$1,624; truck 2016 F-150 5.0L, $15.99-$45.00 + 3.7-7.3 hr = about $460-$1,213; luxury 2015 BMW 328i, parts $27.99-$58.10 but no total can be built because no stated labor time was found. The seal is $16-$58 on every example, so the bill is almost all labor for taking the transmission out and putting it back. The bottom: the only total near $400 is a two-wheel-drive truck at about $460, and that rests on a weak second-hand book time; every front-wheel-drive car we could build starts near $690, and the three benchmarks start at $600-$650. A floor nearer $600 fits cars better, with about $450 possible only on a simple two-wheel-drive truck. The top: our highest built total is about $1,624 (a midsize car at 10 hours and $160 an hour), and Endurance puts trucks and SUVs at up to $2,000 and luxury vehicles at $1,500-$3,000, so $1,925 is reasonable for mainstream vehicles and may be low for luxury and four-wheel-drive ones; we could not confirm that with a stated time. What is null and why: both luxury hour figures. A second search on 2026-11-19 still found no BMW or other luxury bulletin that prints a rear main seal time: GM's Cadillac figures of 15-18 hours include a thrust bearing and oil pan work, a Mercedes bulletin left its labor table empty, a Ford bulletin covering the Lincoln MKX, Nautilus and Aviator rear seal is information-only with no time, and a Lexus oil-leak bulletin leaves the time blank. The nearest manufacturer figure is 4.1 hours to replace flexplate bolts on a 2025 Grand Wagoneer, which is the same transmission-out access but not a seal replacement, so it is not used; it only suggests that luxury labor starts above four hours. No BMW time units were converted. Benchmarks: three, but the third (ThePricer) is a general consumer pricing site, not a repair-industry source; the RepairPal estimate pages for this job loaded without their figures, and no Jerry, Kelley Blue Book or YourMechanic price for it was found. How solid the labor times are: weak overall. The one manufacturer time for an actual rear main seal replacement is FCA's 5.6 hours for a 2024-2025 Jeep Compass 1.3L, used as the low end for economy and midsize although it is neither example vehicle. The economy high (7.4 hr) is GM's time for the Cruze itself but for a neighboring repair that needs the same transmission and flexplate removal. The midsize high (10 hr) is a general statement in a signed article. The truck figures (3.7 and 7.3 hr) are unsigned second-hand book times for a 1997 Dodge Dakota from a question page, supported by a similar reply giving 3.8-6.7 hours for a Ford Sport Trac and, on the manufacturer side, by FCA's 4.0 hours for flexplate bolts on a 2025 Ram 1500 (the same access work, not the seal); no manufacturer-stated seal time for a pickup was found, because the GM and Ford truck bulletins on this repair print no time. So none of the six hour figures is a stated seal time for the example vehicle. Parts sourcing is also thin for midsize (one priced page for the example). Four-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive vehicles, and engines where the seal comes only with its housing, will run above these totals. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis to confirm the leak really is the rear main seal (oil from a valve cover, oil pan gasket or oil pressure switch runs to the same spot, and a clogged crankcase ventilation system can push oil past a good seal), transmission fluid to top up or replace, engine oil and filter, shop supplies and sales tax. Related parts often quoted at the same time, because the transmission is already out: a seal housing or retainer plate and its gasket, new flexplate or flywheel bolts, the transmission front pump seal, an oil pan gasket, and on manual cars a clutch, pilot bearing or flywheel. Four-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive vehicles add time for the transfer case and driveshafts.
